title: Gate G4 quantified: 'subgroup generated by factors contains −1' vs 'subset product hits −1' disagree in ~20% of (p, C) pairs
connection: Sanity computation: for primes p < 3000 (p ≡ 1 mod 4) and C < 40, the subgroup generated by the prime factors of 4Cp+1 in (ℤ/4C)^× contains −1 but no subset product (with multiplicities) equals −1 in 1695 of 8229 cases (~21%). So the 'Galois/subgroup' relaxation is far from tight: multiplicity (few factors) matters a lot.
why: Quantifies the repo's gate G4 ('class, not parity'): any proof via 'some prime factor lands outside a subgroup' loses ~20% of the certificates per C, which matters when the expected count per C is < 1.
first_step: Break down the 21% by ω(4Cp+1) (expect: mostly ω ≤ 2); check whether for ω ≥ 4 the two notions agree ≥ 95%; if so, 'C with 4Cp+1 having ≥ 4 prime factors' is a regime where the Galois relaxation is essentially exact.

title: Finding/lemma: every C-form certificate divisor a of 4Cp+1 is a quadratic non-residue mod p ((a/p) = −1), and this reproves T1 for the C-form
connection: If a | 4Cp+1 with a ≡ −1 (mod 4C) then 4Cp ≡ −1 (mod a), so (4Cp/a) = (−1/a) = −1 (a ≡ 3 mod 4). Quadratic reciprocity gives (C/a) = +1 for a ≡ −1 (mod 4C) (odd part: (C′/a) = (a/C′)(−1)^{(C′−1)/2} = (−1/C′)(−1)^{(C′−1)/2} = 1; 2-part: a ≡ 7 mod 8 when 8 | a+1 so (2/a) = 1). Hence (p/a) = −1 and, as p ≡ 1 mod 4, (a/p) = −1. Verified for all 1798 certificates with p < 3000, C < 80. For p = m² this is impossible ((a/m²) = +1): T1 in two lines. The cofactor b = (4Cp+1)/a is also a QNR mod p (b ≡ a^{−1} mod p).
why: A necessary condition on certificates that is *not* a residue condition on C alone — it couples a with p. It halves the candidate divisors and suggests the exceptional primes (409, 577, 5569, 9601) may be explained by a further forced symbol. It also makes the C-form a purely 'QNR-divisor' problem: find C with a QNR (mod p) divisor a ≡ −1 (mod 4C) of 4Cp+1.
first_step: Do the same computation for full Type II (f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 mod 4cd, ff′ = 4c²dp+1): is (f/p) forced? (Expect (f/p) = (−d/·)-twisted.) Then for Type I. Then try to use the QNR condition positively: among divisors a ≡ −1 mod 4C of 4Cp+1, QR and QNR mod p should be equidistributed by a Pólya–Vinogradov-type argument over C — i.e. the condition costs a factor 1/2, no more.

title: Meta: maintain a single 'dictionary of forms' table (Type I, Type II, C-form, e-slice, word, ES₅, U_n, quaternion) with exact equivalence scopes
connection: This lane found that one popular form (C-form) is strictly weaker than Type II; the repo has ≥ 8 reformulations and their mutual implications are scattered. A one-page table 'form A ⟹ form B (scope, proof pointer, counterexample if not ⟺)' prevents wasted lanes.
why: Cheap, high-leverage: half the items in any breadth lane depend on which form they silently assume.
first_step: Create REFORMULATIONS.md with a matrix of implications among the 8 forms, each entry with a pointer or a small counterexample (e.g. 409 for C-form vs Type II).

title: Meta: a standing 'calibration suite' of hard primes for any proposed mechanism
connection: Fix once a list: adversarial primes (DISPROOF_AVENUES), pseudosquare primes, C-form exceptions (409, 577, 5569, 9601), odd squares (must FAIL for Type I/II mechanisms), U(n) sporadics, near-squares. Every new idea is run on the suite first.
why: Turns the T1 test and the adversarial data into a reusable regression test; 10 minutes per idea instead of a lane.
first_step: Write data/calibration_suite.json with the lists and a script that, given a 'mechanism' function p ↦ certificate-or-None, reports hits/misses per category.

title: Meta: switch the primary object from 'f(p) ≥ 1' to 'the failure set F_K = {p : no certificate with parameters ≤ K}' and study F_K as K grows
connection: F_K is a well-defined, computable set for each K; ES says ∩_K F_K ∩ primes = ∅. The sequence F_K (density, structure, smallest elements, Legendre profiles) is a richer object than f(p) and directly mirrors 'squares + sporadic' phenomena (F_∞ ⊇ odd squares).
why: Reframing from 'count' to 'nested exceptional sets' matches how Rickards–Stange and HKRS state results and may expose structure (e.g. F_K is eventually a union of thin sets).
first_step: Compute F_K for K = 1..50 (parameter = c²d or C) on n ≤ 10⁶ (all n); plot density vs K; list the structure of F_50.

title: Meta: run the board on the single question 'what structure must the exceptional set F_∞ have if nonempty?' (disproof-side reasoning)
connection: Instead of asking how to prove ES, ask the dual: suppose F_∞ ∩ primes ≠ ∅; derive necessary properties of such a prime (all 4c²dp+1 have factors in −1-free subgroups mod 4cd for all (c,d) ≤ K; Legendre profile; size). Then check whether those properties are self-contradictory for p large (a sieve upper bound on 'prime constellations' of unbounded length).
why: The 'unbounded constellation' angle (item in batch 3) may be the cleanest potential contradiction: no prime can have 4c²dp+1 'nearly prime in a subgroup sense' for ALL (c,d) ≤ K with K → ∞ unless the subgroup condition is 'cheap' — quantify.
first_step: Write the necessary conditions for p ∈ F_K formally; estimate via sieve the number of p ≤ X in F_K; see if the estimate goes to 0 faster than 1 for K ≈ log X (that's the heuristic) and whether any step is provable.

title: Meta: crowd-source via Polymath-style wiki a 'census of all known identities with their residue scope'
connection: Mordell, Salez, Cao–Xu (56 families), repo identity census: there is no unified machine-readable list. A JSON file (family, parameters, residue classes covered, type) enables all covering/complement computations in seconds.
why: Foundational tooling; the Cao–Xu 56 families (unverified) can be machine-verified in the process.
first_step: Parse Cao–Xu 2610.32302's families into JSON; verify each symbolically (sympy) and compute the union of residue classes mod 840·k covered.

title: Meta: adopt 'squares + sporadic' as the official conjecture shape for Type II alone and for Type I alone
connection: Instead of ES itself, state: 'f_II(n) = 0 iff n is an odd square or n ∈ S_II (finite)'; similarly Type I. These are stronger, type-separated conjectures with their own sporadic lists, cheaper to test, and their mechanism (reciprocity obstruction only at squares) is more precisely what HKRS/RS handle.
why: Separating types might reveal that one type has a *provable* 'squares + sporadic' structure (e.g. Type I via class-group/ternary-form theory, Duke–Schulze-Pillot style) even if the other doesn't.
first_step: Compute S_I and S_II (n ≤ 10⁷, all n) and see if they stabilise; then check Type I's structure against representation-by-ternary-forms theorems.

title: Experimental: histogram of (c, d) parameter pairs of ALL Type I solutions across primes — is the (c,d) 'mass' concentrated on few d?
connection: If most Type I solutions have d ∈ {1,2,3,5,…} small, then Type I is essentially a handful of imaginary quadratic fields; the per-d problem (class group of ℚ(√−d) fixed) is more rigid.
why: Reduces 'infinitely many (c,d)' to 'finitely many d with c varying' for the bulk of certificates — a dimension reduction for proofs.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶, tabulate the fraction of primes whose FIRST Type I solution has d ≤ 10, and the fraction with ANY d ≤ 10 solution.

title: Experimental: 'd = 1 ∪ d = 2 ∪ d = 3' — do three fixed imaginary quadratic fields already certify all primes ≤ 10⁸ (Type I)?
connection: If yes, ES on that range follows from three class-group-structured problems; the question 'is there a p with no Type I solution for d ≤ 3' becomes the sharpened target with full algebraic structure (ℤ[i], ℤ[√−2], ℤ[ω]).
why: Fixed-field problems admit Chebotarev/ray-class analysis; a fixed finite set of fields with 'all p' coverage would be a new, cleaner conjecture.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10⁷ whether a Type I certificate with d ∈ {1,2,3} exists (c unbounded up to p); list failures and their count growth.

title: Experimental: 'second-smallest certificate' statistics — gaps between the first and second winning parameters
connection: If the second certificate typically appears soon after the first (small ratio), solutions cluster; if far, they are 'isolated events'. Clustering suggests a local structure around certificates (a 'neighbourhood rule' generating one from another).
why: Cheap, and a neighbourhood rule would be a dynamical structure.
first_step: Compute (C₂/C₁) for the two smallest winning parameters for p ≤ 10⁶; histogram.

title: Experimental: do certificates for p and for p' = p + 4Ck share structure when 4Cp+1 and 4Cp'+1 share factors?
connection: 4Cp' + 1 = 4Cp + 1 + 16C²k; sharing a divisor a requires 16C²k ≡ 0 mod a. So certificates with divisor a propagate along p ≡ p₀ (mod a) — the covering class. This is the 'template reuse' structure; the experiment is to measure how far a single template's class extends (its density of primes actually certified = 1/a · (all primes in the class) — trivially all? YES: if a | 4Cp+1 and a ≡ −1 mod 4C then for every p' ≡ p mod a, a | 4Cp'+1 too, and the cofactor b' = (4Cp'+1)/a ≡ ? mod 4C: 4Cp'+1 ≡ 1 mod 4C, a ≡ −1 ⟹ b' ≡ −1 ✓.) So each (C, a) certifies the entire class p ≡ −(4C)^{−1} mod a. Record as a lemma.
why: This is exactly the covering-system structure of the C-form: each certificate is a residue class of modulus a ≡ −1 (mod 4C). ES (C-form part) ⟺ primes ⊂ ∪ classes. Make the lemma explicit; cross-check with the exceptional primes 409 etc. (they lie in no class with a ≤ 6000 or so).
first_step: Write the one-line proof; then for the exceptions, compute for a ≤ 10⁵ whether p ≡ −(4C)^{−1} mod a for some a ≡ −1 mod 4C — the same as C-form search but organised by a.

title: Erdős covering-system theory: the C-form classes have moduli a ≡ −1 (mod 4C) for each C — density of the union by Erdős–Selfridge-style inclusion–exclusion
connection: The union over C and a ≡ −1 (4C) of the classes r_{C,a} mod a: its lower density is computable; Erdős's covering theory and the 'density of a union of residue classes' (Rogers/Simpson, and the Hough–Nielsen bound) describe how large a union of classes with distinct moduli can be. Here moduli repeat? (Different C can give the same a: a ≡ −1 mod 4C and mod 4C′ means lcm | a + 1.)
why: If the natural density of the union over all (C, a) with a ≤ A is 1 − o(1) as A → ∞ at a provable rate, then the C-form certifies 'almost all' integers in a quantified way — comparable to Vaughan but elementary; the rate's dependence on the Legendre profile would explain the exceptions.
first_step: Compute lower bound density via Bonferroni for a ≤ A, A = 10³..10⁵; compare with the empirical density of integers ≤ 10⁷ having a C-form certificate with a ≤ A.

title: Probability: ES failure as the event that a 'random' prime avoids infinitely many independent residue classes — a Borel–Cantelli on the covering classes
connection: If p's residues mod a (for a ≡ −1 mod 4C) were independent uniform, P(p avoids class r_{C,a} for all (C,a) ≤ K) = Π (1 − 1/a) ≈ exp(−Σ 1/a) → 0 as K → ∞ since Σ_{a ≡ −1 (4C)} 1/a diverges (like (1/φ(4C)) log). Borel–Cantelli direction 'infinitely many events occur a.s.' — the point is that for ONE p the events are deterministic, but the independence heuristic says failure is impossible; a rigorous version is the Kubilius model / Turán–Kubilius for 'residues of p across moduli'.
why: The Kubilius model gives rigorous approximation of arithmetic functions by independent random variables *on average over p*; its pointwise version is the Erdős–Kac-type concentration. Here we need 'for each p' — but a Turán–Kubilius variance bound over p ∈ [X, 2X] gives that the number of p ≤ X avoiding all classes ≤ K is ≪ X·exp(−c log K) + error; with K ≈ X^ε this is the Vaughan-type exceptional set bound by elementary means. Re-derive and compare constants.
first_step: Do the Turán–Kubilius-style second-moment calculation for the C-form classes; compare the resulting E(N) bound with Vaughan's; note any slack.
refs: Kubilius, Probabilistic methods in the theory of numbers

title: Probability: Lovász Local Lemma for 'p avoids all classes' — dependency graph of the events across (C, a)
connection: LLL gives existence of an outcome avoiding all 'bad' events when each has small probability and few dependencies; here we want the OPPOSITE (no p avoids all good events), i.e. LLL would be used to show a counterexample is *consistent* — a disproof-side consistency check. Compute the dependency structure: events E_{C,a} = {p ≡ r mod a} for different a are dependent only via CRT (independent for coprime moduli!).
why: Since residues mod coprime moduli are 'independent' in the CRT sense, the LLL/CRT construction shows there exist INTEGERS avoiding any finite collection of classes (as long as the classes don't cover) — but primality is the constraint that breaks the construction; so a counterexample must exist as an integer for each finite K (trivial: odd squares!) and ES hinges on primality + infinitely many K. Record precisely as a 'what the problem is' statement.
first_step: Note that odd squares are integers avoiding ALL classes (T1); so the integer version of 'avoid all' has solutions; ES is about primes. Write up the distinction and the role of primality in the C-form: p prime enters only via... nothing?! The C-form condition 4Cp+1 = ab makes no use of p's primality — so the C-form conjecture 'every non-square n has a C-form certificate' is the right integer statement, and its exceptions (409, 577, 5569, 9601 among primes; plus composites?) are the data.

title: Composite exceptions to the C-form: which non-square n < 10⁵ have no 4Cn+1 = ab, a ≡ b ≡ −1 (4C)?
connection: The C-form does not use primality, so it's a statement about all n. Odd squares fail (T1). Which other n fail? Among primes 409, 577, 5569, 9601 (C < 1500). Composite failures would show whether the C-form exceptional set is 'squares + sporadic' or has infinite non-square families.
why: Cheap census that characterises a natural sub-conjecture; the structure of composite exceptions (do they factor as square × something? products of C-form exceptions?) is informative.
first_step: Compute for all n ≤ 10⁵ (n ≡ 1 mod 4; also check n ≡ 3 mod 4 which has a different parity structure) whether a C-form certificate exists with C ≤ 2000; list non-square failures; factor them.

title: Why do 409 and 577 fail the C-form? Attempt a T1-style local proof
connection: 409 = 20² + 3², 577 = 24² + 1 = 24² + 1²; both are 'one more than a multiple of a square'? 577 = 576 + 1 = 24² + 1; 409 = 400 + 9; 5569 = 5568 + 1 = ? (5568 = 2⁶·87) no; 9601 = 9600 + 1 = 2⁷·75 + 1 ≈ (98)² = 9604 so 9601 = 98² − 3. 577 = 24² + 1 and 9601 = 98² − 3, 409 = 20² + 9, 5569 = 74² + 93? 74² = 5476, 75² = 5625; so 5569 = 5625 − 56. Hmm no pattern. A local obstruction would be: for all C, every divisor a of 4Cp+1 with a ≡ −1 (4C) violates a Jacobi symbol identity — as in T1 but for specific p. If none exists, the exceptions are 'finite-C accidents' and a certificate exists for some larger C.
why: Either outcome is informative: a new local obstruction at non-squares (contradicting the 'squares only' heuristic for the C-form) or an upper bound on C_min for these primes (so C_min is unbounded in a quantified way).
first_step: Search C up to 10⁶ for p ∈ {409, 577, 5569, 9601} with efficient trial (factor 4Cp+1 via sympy or Pari); if found, record C_min; if not, attempt the Jacobi-symbol argument.

title: Analytic: the C-form expected count Σ_{C ≤ X} E[#{a | 4Cp+1 : a ≡ −1 (4C)}] ≈ Σ_C τ(4Cp+1)/φ(4C) — compare with Type II's Σ_{c,d}
connection: Full Type II has modulus 4cd and N = 4c²dp+1: expected count Σ_{c,d} τ(4c²dp+1)/φ(4cd) — summing over c with fixed d gives an extra log factor (Σ_c 1/φ(4cd) diverges like log). So full Type II has expected count ≍ log p·log²X vs the C-form's log p·log X: the c-parameter is where the extra log in log²p comes from. This explains why the C-form misses some primes (its count is smaller by a log).
why: Quantifies the exceptional-prime phenomenon just observed; and it suggests the (c,d) structure is not decorative: the c-direction provides a *second* log, which is the 'thickness' separating 'almost all' from 'all'? (B3 still says polylog.)
first_step: Compute the expected counts numerically for p ≈ 10⁶ and ranges X ≤ 10³: C-form vs Type II vs Type I; confirm the extra log factor.

title: Recreational: the 'Egyptian fraction game' (players alternately subtract unit fractions from 4/n; last mover wins) — its P-positions
connection: Combinatorial game whose P-positions are governed by the two-term representability of remainders; ES is 'the first player can win in 3 moves'. Game-theoretic analysis (Sprague–Grundy) of unit-fraction subtraction games may have been studied.
why: Recreational lens; may surface a known structural result on unit-fraction subtraction.
first_step: Search 'unit fraction subtraction game Sprague–Grundy'; compute Grundy values for 4/n with n ≤ 200.

title: Puzzle: 'three resistors/three lenses' puzzle submissions to recreational columns (Gardner, Dudeney) — any that is ES in disguise with a slick solution for a sub-case?
connection: Dudeney-style puzzles on 'divide a quantity into three unit-fraction parts' exist; a slick trick for a sub-case (e.g. n ≡ 2 mod 3) might be an identity not in Mordell's list.
why: Low probability, cheap.
first_step: Search 'Dudeney unit fractions three' and 'Gardner Egyptian fractions 4/n'; skim.

title: Mathematical-olympiad lens: known olympiad problems 'show 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z for n ≡ r mod m' and their solutions as identity sources
connection: Many olympiad/Putnam problems ask for specific residue classes (e.g. n ≡ 2 mod 3, n ≡ 3 mod 4); their solutions are identities already in Mordell's list, but the *techniques* (e.g. choosing x = (n+1)/2…) occasionally differ.
why: Cheap; the AoPS archive is searchable.
first_step: Search AoPS for 'Erdős–Straus' and '4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z'; collect all identities; diff against the repo census.

title: Probabilistic number theory: model the prime factors of 4c²dp+1 across (c,d) as a Poisson–Dirichlet process and compute the exact 'failure probability' at fixed p
connection: Poisson–Dirichlet models the relative sizes of prime factors of a random integer; combined with residue classes equidistributed, it gives the probability that the subset-product set misses −1 mod 4cd. Summing log of (1 − P) over (c,d) gives a refined heuristic exp(−c·log²p)… the refinement tells which (c,d) carry most of the 'mass'.
why: A sharper heuristic that identifies the dominant (c,d) region makes targeted provable sub-statements possible (e.g. 'the (c,d) with d = 1 and c ≤ log²p already give expected count ≥ 1').
first_step: Simulate: for p ≈ 10¹⁸ (no factoring needed — sample Poisson–Dirichlet factorisations), estimate P(fail at (c,d)) for (c,d) ≤ 100; sum.

title: Analogy: Goldbach's 'every even n is p + q' vs ES's 'every p has a certificate' — the Hardy–Littlewood singular series as the ES 'local factor' and its *minimum* over p
connection: For Goldbach the singular series S(n) ≥ 1 > 0 uniformly; for ES, the analogous local product (over small primes q of the local solution density) could in principle degenerate for some p — a 'local near-obstruction' that makes certain p hard. Compute the min of S_ES(p) over p and see whether it correlates with small f(p).
why: If min_p S_ES(p) is bounded below (like Goldbach), hardness is purely 'global'; if S_ES(p) → 0 along a subsequence (near-squares?), that's a local mechanism for hard primes worth understanding.
first_step: Define S_ES(p) = Π_{q ≤ Q} (local density of (c,d,f) solutions mod q normalised); compute for p ≤ 10⁶; correlate with f(p).

title: Analogy: Waring's problem G(k) — every large n is a sum of s k-th powers; the 'every n' is forced by the circle method's major arcs dominating. ES's 'major arc' is M_BM; its 'minor arcs' are uncontrolled — can a circle method over the (c,d)-torus be set up at all?
connection: Write the certificate count as ∫ Σ_{c,d,f} e(α(stuff)) dα: the Type II equation ff′ − 4c²dp = 1 is a single Diophantine equation in (f, f′, c, d) with p fixed — a 4-variable equation of degree 4 (f·f′ − 4c²d·p); the circle method needs many variables relative to degree, and here the number of variables is 4 and the 'size' is tied to p. Birch's condition fails spectacularly. Quantify.
why: Even a clear 'why the circle method cannot work here' is useful; but there might be a variant (e.g. Kloosterman refinement, delta method of Duke–Friedlander–Iwaniec) that handles equations like ff′ − D = 1 with congruences — these are 'shifted convolution' sums, which DFI's delta method handles with few variables!
first_step: Write the Type II count as a shifted convolution Σ_{ff′ = 4c²dp + 1} with congruences, and check the delta-method literature (DFI 1993; Heath-Brown's version) for the needed uniformity in p.
refs: Heath-Brown, 'A new form of the circle method' (1996)

title: Quadratic divisor problem (DFI): Σ τ(n) τ(n + h) and Σ τ(an + b)… the ES count as a 'twisted divisor sum along a quadratic sequence'
connection: Type I: Σ_c #{f | p² + 4c²d, f ≡ −p (4cd)} is a divisor sum along the quadratic polynomial 4dc² + p² in c, with a residue condition tied to c. Divisor sums along quadratic polynomials (Hooley's Σ τ(n² + 1), and the general theory for Σ τ(f(n)) by Hooley, Bykovskii, and recent work by Browning / Sofos) have asymptotics with power savings — *for the unrestricted sum*.
why: The unrestricted Σ_{c ≤ X} τ(p² + 4c²d) has a known asymptotic (Hooley-type) with explicit dependence on the polynomial's discriminant (−16dp²... depends on p!). Pointwise-in-p control of the error is exactly the uniformity question; the literature's dependence on the coefficients is explicit enough to check.
first_step: Read Hooley 'On the number of divisors of quadratic polynomials' (Acta Math 1963) and extract the uniformity in the polynomial's coefficients; apply to p² + 4dc² with X ≈ p^θ.

title: Experimental mathematics: the 'Ramanujan-style' approach — find exact identities among ES counts and classical arithmetic functions by brute-force linear algebra (Wilf–Zeilberger-free)
connection: Compute vectors (f_I(n), f_II(n), f(n), τ(n), σ(n), r₂(n), r₄(n), h(−4n), H(4n−1)…) for n ≤ 2000 and search for integer linear/bilinear relations via LLL on the data matrix. Any exact relation (even conjectural) is structural gold.
why: Standard experimental-math technique; cheap; a positive hit would redirect the campaign.
first_step: Build the matrix, run PSLQ/LLL for relations with small coefficients among ≤ 10 functions; validate hits on n ≤ 10⁵.

title: Experimental: generating-function fitting — is Σ f_II(n) q^n a quasi-modular form up to a small error?
connection: Test numerically whether the q-series of ES counts (or sub-counts) is close to a combination of Eisenstein series E₂, E₄ and theta functions: compute the coefficients, fit by least squares to a basis of modular forms of small weight/level, check residuals.
why: If a sub-count is quasi-modular, its coefficients have asymptotic formulas with explicit error (Deligne/Rankin–Selberg), potentially pointwise; a quick fit is the test.
first_step: Compute f_II(n) for n ≤ 5000; fit to the space spanned by divisor-sum functions σ_k(n), σ_k(n/2), r_k(n); report residual norm.

title: Experimental: Benford / leading-digit and last-digit statistics of certificates (a, b) to detect hidden multiplicative structure
connection: If the divisor a in 4Cp+1 = ab were 'random' among divisors, its log would be arcsine-distributed; deviations from arcsine would show the residue condition biases size (e.g. a ≈ √N preferred?).
why: Size bias reveals which divisors win — relevant to choosing weights and to Lenstra's 'large modulus ⟹ few divisors' regime.
first_step: Histogram log a / log N for all certificates of p ≤ 10⁶; compare with arcsine.

title: Pure analogy: Erdős's '2^n mod n' and 'p + 2^k' problems vs ES — the 'exponential reservoir' difference
connection: Problems with reservoir 2^k (k ≤ log N: only log N candidates) are like ES (polylog candidates) and remain open (p + 2^k not covering an AP — proved by Erdős via covering congruences!). Erdős's covering construction PROVES failure of 'every odd n is p + 2^k' — a negative result via coverings. For ES, is there a covering-congruence construction showing that some explicit residue class of n has NO solution of a restricted shape (e.g. with max(x,y,z) ≤ n²)? That would be a 'restricted-ES is false' result, calibrating which restrictions are safe.
why: Erdős's covering-congruence method is the standard way to prove 'polylog-reservoir' problems FAIL on an AP; applying it to restricted versions of ES tells which restrictions (bounds on x,y,z; Type I only; d = 1 only) are provably insufficient.
first_step: Try to construct a covering of ℤ by classes n ≡ r_i (mod m_i) such that each class forces 'no Type I solution with d = 1' (via a local obstruction like T1 but for the class); if achievable, 'd = 1 Type I' is provably not a complete mechanism on an AP.

title: Sieve of Eratosthenes generalisation: 'sieve by certificates' — remove from [1, X] all n certified by (C, a) with a ≤ A; what remains?
connection: The uncovered integers after sieving by all C-form classes with a ≤ A form a 'sifted set'; its density and the structure of its elements as A grows are exactly computable; compare with the sieve-theoretic prediction Π (1 − 1/a) — the discrepancy measures the correlation structure (classes are not independent).
why: A direct empirical measure of the 'independence' heuristic, which underlies the exp(−log²p) prediction; strong positive correlation would mean failures cluster (good for proofs: fewer independent events to control).
first_step: Compute the sifted set for X = 10⁶ and A up to 10⁴; compare its size with the independence prediction; inspect the residue structure of survivors.

title: Large sieve inequality applied to the exceptional set with the C-form classes as the sifting classes
connection: Classical large sieve: if a set S ⊂ [1, X] avoids ω(q) residue classes mod q for each q ≤ Q, then |S| ≤ (X + Q²)/L with L = Σ_{q ≤ Q} μ²(q) Π_{p|q} ω(p)/(p − ω(p)). For the C-form, S = exceptional set avoids, for each prime a ≡ −1 (mod 4C), the single class r_{C,a} mod a — ω(a) = #{C : 4C | a + 1} = τ((a+1)/4)-ish. So L ≈ Σ_{a ≤ Q} #{C: 4C | a+1}/a ≈ Σ_a τ((a+1)/4)/a ≈ (1/2) log²Q. Hence |exceptions ≤ X| ≪ (X + Q²)/log²Q — with Q = √X: ≪ X/log²X. A quick, elementary exceptional-set bound; weaker than Vaughan but *structurally* it shows the exceptional set has density 0 with a log² saving that mirrors the log²p count.
why: Elementary, and its proof shape (large sieve with ω(a) ~ τ(a+1)) might extend to a *weighted* large sieve giving more; and it exhibits ES's exceptional-set bounds as a special case of sieving by 'divisor-many' classes.
first_step: Verify the computation of L carefully (sum over prime a only, or all a via the full large sieve with multiplicative ω); compare with Vaughan's exp(−c(log N)^{2/3}); check whether larger Q (via Montgomery–Vaughan with Q up to X^{1/2}) or Type II's extra (c,d) classes improve the exponent.
refs: Montgomery, 'The analytic principle of the large sieve' (1978)

title: Gallagher's larger sieve for the ES exceptional set: exploit that exceptions avoid MANY classes mod each a
connection: Gallagher's larger sieve is efficient when the sifted set avoids most classes mod each prime (ω(q) close to q); ES exceptions avoid only one class per (C, a) — so Gallagher is wrong tool; but for the full Type II family, a given a is a modulus for many (c,d) (all with 4cd | a + 1) with DIFFERENT classes r_{c,d,a} = −(4c²d)^{−1} mod a, so the number of avoided classes mod a is #{(c,d): 4cd | a+1} ≈ τ-many distinct classes (are they distinct? −(4c²d)^{-1} for different (c,d) with the same cd... c²d = c·(cd), so different c with the same cd give different classes). Still ≪ a, so the larger sieve doesn't bite. Record as negative.
why: Closes a door cheaply, and the count of 'distinct avoided classes per modulus a' is itself the key quantity for any sieve bound — tabulate it.
first_step: For a ≤ 10⁴, compute ω(a) = #{distinct classes −(4c²d)^{-1} mod a over (c,d) with 4cd | a+1}; its average order vs a.

title: Brun–Titchmarsh-type pointwise bound in the other direction: upper bounds on f(p) (every p has ≤ C log²p?) and what they teach
connection: Upper bounds for f(p) are pointwise and provable (τ-type bounds give f(p) ≪ p^ε; sharper ≪ log^A p?). The methods for pointwise UPPER bounds (divisor bound, Lenstra's ≤ 11 per large modulus) when examined might show where the lower bound fails symmetrically.
why: Calibration: is f(p) ≪ (log p)^A pointwise provable? If yes, the certificates are 'thin' both ways, and the problem is a two-sided concentration with only the lower side open.
first_step: Search 'upper bound number of solutions 4/n three unit fractions pointwise'; try to prove f(p) ≪ p^ε from divisor bounds and see if log-power is attainable via Lenstra's result (moduli 4cd > N^{1/3}).

title: ML: contrastive learning of 'certificate embeddings' to cluster primes by solution structure
connection: Embed each prime by the multiset of its certificate parameters {(c,d)} (as a bag-of-words), cluster, and inspect clusters' arithmetic properties (residues, Legendre profiles). Clusters = 'types of primes' with similar mechanisms.
why: Unsupervised structure discovery; cheap; if clusters align with Legendre profiles it supports the 'Legendre identities' direction.
first_step: Build the feature bags for p ≤ 10⁵; TF-IDF + k-means/UMAP; test cluster–residue alignment via mutual information.

title: ML: train a model to predict f(p) from the factorisations of 4Cp+1, C ≤ 20, to measure how much of f is 'explained' by small C
connection: f(p) is a sum over all (c,d); regressing f(p) on small-parameter data tells what fraction of the count (and of the variance) is small-parameter — if ~90%, the problem is 'nearly local' in parameter space.
why: Dimension-reduction evidence; directs effort to small-parameter theory (class groups of small d) if the fraction is high.
first_step: Compute f(p) and the small-parameter sub-count for p ≤ 10⁶; R² of the regression; plot residuals.

title: Formal: state and prove in Lean the C-form ⟹ ES implication and the T1 obstruction (odd squares have no C-form certificate)
connection: Two small, self-contained theorems; T1's reciprocity proof is a good test of mathlib's Jacobi symbol API.
why: Produces citable formalised lemmas and might reveal a slicker proof of T1 (formalisation often does).
first_step: Write the Lean statements; prove the C-form ⟹ solution direction (pure algebra); attempt T1 via `jacobiSym` lemmas.

title: Formal: Lean-verify the Mordell cover (all n not in the 6 square classes mod 840 have solutions) as a decidable computation + identities
connection: A formal proof that ES reduces to the 6 square classes mod 840 (a finite check of identities) would be a clean mathlib contribution and the base for any future formal work.
why: Cheap-ish, high visibility; could attract Lean community collaborators to ES.
first_step: Encode Mordell's identities as Lean lemmas `∀ k, 4/(840k + r) = …` for each covered r; use `decide` over residues.

title: Reverse direction: from the exceptional-prime data, construct 'ES-hard' pseudo-random primes by CRT to stress-test at 10²⁰ (profile engineering)
connection: Take the Legendre profiles of the C-form exceptions and of the adversarial primes; construct primes ≈ 10²⁰ with the same profile mod all primes ≤ 50 (CRT + primality search); measure f(p). If the profile predicts hardness, we've found a 'hardness invariant'; if not, hardness is not profile-driven.
why: Direct test of the Legendre-profile hypothesis, which underlies several items here.
first_step: Compute profiles of 409, 577, 5569, 9601 and the repo's hardest primes; CRT-construct 100 primes near 10¹⁵ per profile; compute Type I/II counts on small parameters.

title: Analogy with 'every integer is a sum of 3 triangular numbers' (Gauss) — a ternary representation theorem proved via class numbers; ES as a 'ternary' problem whose class-number formula is missing
connection: Gauss's Eureka theorem = r₃(8n+3) > 0 via h(−(8n+3)) > 0 — positivity of a class number! ES's Type I count at fixed d is governed by divisors of p² + 4c²d, i.e. by representations in ℚ(√−d); the analogue of 'h > 0' is the existence of an ideal of norm f in the right ray class — i.e., SURJECTIVITY of the Artin map onto a ray class group, which is Chebotarev-existence again.
why: Clarifies that ES's 'positivity' is of Artin-map-surjectivity type (every ray class contains an ideal dividing a specific (p + 2c√−d)) — a statement about ONE element's factorisation, hence B2; but it suggests looking at the *family over c* as a family of principal ideals (p + 2c√−d) whose ideal factors sweep the ray class group as c varies: do they equidistribute in the ray class group mod 4cd? (The modulus grows with c — a 'tied' equidistribution.)
first_step: For d = 1, p fixed, c ≤ X: compute the ray classes (mod 4c) of the ideal factors of (p + 2ci) in ℤ[i]; test equidistribution across c; identify the class containing the certificate.
refs: Cox, Primes of the form x² + ny²

title: Tied equidistribution: factors of (p + 2c√−d) in ray class groups of conductor 4cd as c varies — a 'horizontal Chebotarev' with growing conductor

(Reminiscent of 'p splits completely in K_n for infinitely many n' questions, Iwasawa theory, and of Kummer-type 'order of p mod n' statistics: p's residue mod n as n varies is equidistributed trivially; but the ideal factorisation of p + 2c√−d mod 4c is like 'p's behaviour in the ray class field', not controlled by p alone.)

title: Artin's primitive-root conjecture (Hooley, GRH) as the model for 'a fixed p with a property across infinitely many moduli'

The repo's survey may have missed it. The key: Artin needs infinitely many good q and gets density; ES needs ONE good (c,d), which is weaker.

title: Analogy: Lehmer's problem on Euler's totient / 'n | 2^n − 2'-type statements and the 'divisor of a shifted multiple' structure
connection: 'a | 4Cp+1 with a ≡ −1 mod 4C' is a divisor-of-shifted-multiple condition like 'p | 2^{p−1} − 1' (Fermat) or Wieferich; in those, rigidity comes from group orders (Lagrange). Is there a group in which 4Cp+1's divisors arise as orders of elements (so Lagrange forces structure)?
why: If a | 4Cp+1 ⟺ some element has order dividing 4Cp+1 in a group of order a ... (e.g. a | 4Cp+1 ⟺ ord_a(something) | 4Cp+1); then the condition a ≡ −1 mod 4C is about a's group having an element of order a+1/(4C)... Speculative, but 'orders of elements in (ℤ/a)^×' is rigid.
first_step: Note that a | 4Cp+1 ⟺ 4Cp ≡ −1 mod a ⟺ (4C)·p ≡ −1: p ≡ −(4C)^{−1}; no group-order content. Drop unless a different group (e.g. elliptic curve over F_a with a + 1 − t points) gives a + 1 = 4C·(…) — Hasse's theorem: #E(F_a) = a + 1 − t; if #E = a + 1 (supersingular, t = 0) then 4C | #E(F_a) is a condition on the curve, and 'a ≡ −1 mod 4C' ⟺ 4C | a + 1 = #E for supersingular E. Interesting: certificates ⟺ supersingular curves over F_a with 4C | #E and a | 4Cp+1.

title: Elliptic curves with a + 1 points over F_a: supersingular reduction and the condition 4C | a + 1
connection: Following the previous item: a ≡ −1 (mod 4C) ⟺ 4C | a + 1 = #E(F_a) for any supersingular E/F_a (a prime). CM curves y² = x³ − x have supersingular reduction exactly at primes a ≡ 3 mod 4; y² = x³ + 1 at a ≡ 2 mod 3. So 'a ≡ −1 mod 4C' for C = 1 is 'y² = x³ − x is supersingular at a'; for general C it's '4C | #E(F_a)' for supersingular E, i.e. E(F_a) has a point of order 4C (cyclic case). Reformulation: C-form certificate ⟺ a prime a | 4Cp+1 at which some supersingular curve has full 4C-torsion-ish.
why: Likely just a restatement, but it connects to the theory of torsion of reductions (Lang–Trotter, Koblitz-type conjectures), which has GRH-conditional pointwise-in-E results about the density of primes with prescribed #E mod m — again 'fixed object, varying prime' = Artin-type shape.
first_step: Just verify the restatement and note whether Koblitz's conjecture machinery (Zywina) gives anything for primes a dividing a prescribed number 4Cp+1 — no (a is constrained); record as low.

title: Dickson/Schinzel-H-conditional infinite families inside square classes: p such that (4p+1)/5 is a prime ≡ 3 mod 4
connection: If q = (4p+1)/5 is prime with q ≡ 3 mod 4 then 4p+1 = 5q has the divisor q ≡ −1 mod 4 (C = 1) — wait, need a ≡ −1 mod 4C = 4: q ≡ 3 mod 4 ✓. So all such p have C-form certificates. Hypothesis H gives infinitely many primes p with (4p+1)/5 prime in any admissible class; restricted to p in a square class mod 840 (admissible? 4p+1 ≡ 5 mod 3360... need 5 | 4p+1 ⟺ p ≡ 1 mod 5 ✓ compatible with p ≡ 1 mod 840 since 840 = 5·168, p ≡ 1 mod 5 ✓). So: CONDITIONAL on Hypothesis H, there are infinitely many primes in each square class mod 840 satisfying ES via C = 1. Unconditionally: Chen-type sieve gives p with (4p+1)/5 = P₂ (almost prime), not enough (need a factor ≡ 3 mod 4, which a P₂ with both factors ≡ 1 mod 4 lacks).
why: A clean statement of 'conditional infinite families in square classes'; the campaign says no infinite case of ES is proved among hard primes; this item pins the exact unconditional gap: 'infinitely many primes p ≡ 1 mod 840 such that 4p+1 has a prime factor ≡ 3 mod 4' — THIS is a sieve problem (a prime p with 4p+1 having a factor in a residue class) that might be unconditionally provable via sieve + Bombieri–Vinogradov! Check: the set {p : 4p+1 has NO prime factor ≡ 3 mod 4} has density → 0 (like sums of two squares, ~ c/√log x); so infinitely many p ≡ 1 mod 840 with a factor ≡ 3 mod 4 follows from a *lower bound* on primes in the class minus an upper bound on the exceptional subset — the upper bound of Landau type for 4p+1 with p prime needs a sieve (the 'shifted primes with all factors ≡ 1 mod 4' count is ≪ x/(log x)^{3/2} by half-dimensional sieve — PROVABLE).
first_step: Prove: #{p ≤ x, p ≡ 1 (840) : all prime factors of 4p+1 are ≡ 1 mod 4} ≪ x/(log x)^{3/2} via the half-dimensional sieve (Iwaniec) — then since π(x; 840, 1) ≍ x/log x, infinitely many (indeed almost all!) primes p ≡ 1 mod 840 have a C=1 certificate. Check whether the repo already states 'almost all primes in square classes are certified by C = 1' (it surely knows almost-all results, but maybe not this elementary route).

title: Upgrade: 'almost all primes in each square class have a C ≤ K certificate' via a K-fold half-dimensional sieve, with an explicit exponent 3/2 → (1 + K/2)?

Possibly Σ_C 1/φ(4C)·(…) — the convergence/divergence governs whether density 1 or merely positive density follows.

title: Analogy: Zsigmondy/Bang — every a^n − 1 has a primitive prime divisor (n > 6) — a pointwise 'new divisor exists' theorem; its mechanism (cyclotomic factorisation + size) for 4Cp+1?
connection: Bang–Zsigmondy proves existence of a divisor with a prescribed property (primitive) for EVERY n by exhibiting a factor Φ_n(a) that is large and whose prime factors are ≡ 1 mod n (rigid congruence from cyclotomic theory). ES wants a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C of 4Cp+1. Is there a polynomial identity 4Cp+1 = (algebraic factor) with controlled residues when p itself has a special form (p = Φ_m(a)-ish)? For p of the form (a^m − 1)/(a − 1) or similar, 4Cp+1 might factor cyclotomically for suitable C — giving ES for 'repunit-like' primes unconditionally.
why: Would give explicit infinite families (conditional on infinitely many such primes — which is itself open for repunits), but the mechanism (cyclotomic rigidity) is one of the two accepted (R) mechanisms.
first_step: For p = (a^m − 1)/(a − 1) (prime), search small C with 4Cp+1 factoring as a product of cyclotomic-like polynomials in a; e.g. a = 2: p = 2^m − 1 (Mersenne, ≡ 3 mod 4 — easy class!). Try a = 4, 10, and p = a^m + 1 forms.

For p = 2^{2k}+1: 4Cp + 1 = C·2^{2k+2} + 4C + 1; for C = 2^{2k}: = 2^{4k+2} + 2^{2k+2} + 1 = (2^{2k+1} + 2^{k+1} + 1)(2^{2k+1} − 2^{k+1} + 1)? (Aurifeuillean-type factorisation of 4x⁴ + 1 style: x⁴ + x² + 1 = (x² + x + 1)(x² − x + 1) with x = 2^{k+1}: 2^{4k+4} + 2^{2k+2} + 1 — close but not equal; adjust.) Explore Aurifeuillean factorisations giving divisors in the right class.
why: Aurifeuillean factorisations are rigid algebraic identities for special p (not polynomial in p but polynomial in the exponent base) — a loophole in Mordell–Schinzel for special prime families.
first_step: For p = 2^{2k} + 1 (k ≤ 20, prime or not), test C ∈ {2^j} for Aurifeuillean factorisations of 4Cp+1 and check residues mod 4C; generalise to p = a^{2k} + 1.

title: Lucas-sequence divisibility: choose C so that 4Cp+1 is a term of a Lucas sequence U_n(P,Q) whose prime divisors are ≡ ±1 mod n (rank of apparition theory)
connection: Primes dividing U_n have rank of apparition dividing n, which forces q ≡ (D/q) mod n — a rigid congruence on divisors! If 4Cp+1 = U_n(P,Q) for some (P,Q,n) with n related to 4C, then every prime divisor q satisfies q ≡ ±1 mod n, and the sign is a Legendre symbol — exactly the kind of 'divisor in a class' rigidity ES needs. The catch: 4Cp+1 must be a Lucas term — a Diophantine coincidence; but with C free and (P,Q) free there are many chances.
why: A concrete (R)-mechanism (rank of apparition) that produces divisors with prescribed residues; the question is coverage.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁴, search C ≤ 10³, Lucas sequences with |P|,|Q| ≤ 5, n ≤ 30 for 4Cp+1 = U_n(P,Q) or V_n(P,Q); check whether the forced residue gives the ES class.

title: Cyclotomic rigidity directly: primes dividing Φ_m(x) are ≡ 1 mod m (or divide m). Find x, m with Φ_m(x) = 4Cp+1 and m | ... so that divisors ≡ 1 mod m; need ≡ −1 mod 4C though — use Φ_{2m} or the factor structure of x^m + 1
connection: Prime divisors q of x^m + 1 (odd m) satisfy q ≡ 1 mod 2m or q | 2(x+1)... more precisely primitive divisors of x^{2m} − 1 are ≡ 1 mod 2m. To get divisors ≡ −1 mod 4C we need a different rigidity: primes dividing x² + 1 are ≡ 1 mod 4 (wrong sign); primes dividing x² − 2 are ≡ ±1 mod 8; primes dividing x² + 2 are ≡ 1, 3 mod 8 — the '3 mod 8' is ≡ −1 mod 4 but not −1 mod 8. In general, primes dividing a binary form of discriminant D lie in classes determined by (D/q) = 1 — a *set* of classes, never a single class −1 mod 4C unless the genus theory is trivial. So cyclotomic/quadratic-form rigidity gives 'divisors in a SUBGROUP', not in a coset — and −1 mod 4C must be IN that subgroup. For 4C = 8: the subgroup {1,3} mod 8 (from x² + 2) contains 3 ≢ −1; {1,7} (from x² − 2) contains 7 ≡ −1 ✓. So: if 4Cp + 1 = x² − 2 for some x, then every prime factor is ≡ ±1 mod 8, and the product... need a divisor ≡ 7 mod 8 — exists iff some prime factor is ≡ 7 mod 8 (else all ≡ 1). Not forced. Conclusion: quadratic-form rigidity gives subgroup membership, not coset hitting. Record as a structured negative with the one escape: forms whose 'divisor subgroup' is exactly {±1} mod 4C make the problem a parity question.
why: Pinning down that classical rigidity (cyclotomic/quadratic) gives subgroups not cosets, and identifying the parity escape, is a reusable lemma for the 'generator matrix'.
first_step: Write the lemma; then search for binary forms Q with divisor subgroup {±1} ⊂ (ℤ/4C)^× for small C (requires (ℤ/4C)^× to have a large... only C = 1 or 2 work, since index must be φ(4C)/2 for a quadratic form's genus… no: the subgroup of 'split primes' for ℚ(√D) has index 2; {±1} has index φ(4C)/2; equal only if φ(4C) = 4, i.e. 4C ∈ {8, 12}: C = 2, 3). So for C = 2: x² − 2 (divisors ≡ ±1 mod 8); C = 3: x² + 3 (divisors ≡ 1 mod 3 — hmm need ±1 mod 12: primes dividing x² + 3 are ≡ 1 mod 3 i.e. ≡ 1, 7 mod 12 — wrong). Tabulate properly.

title: C = 2 parity escape: if 8p+1 = x² − 2y² then C=2 certificate ⟺ some prime factor ≡ 7 mod 8 — and the number of such factors has a parity formula via the norm from ℚ(√2)
connection: 8p + 1 = N(x + y√2) = x² − 2y²: all prime factors are ≡ ±1 mod 8 (or 2, excluded as 8p+1 odd). The C=2 C-form certificate needs a divisor ≡ 7 mod 8 ⟺ at least one prime factor ≡ 7 mod 8 (since the ≡ 1 ones can't help; and any single ≡ 7 factor is a certificate). Number of ≡ 7 factors (with multiplicity) is even (product ≡ 1 mod 8). So C = 2 wins ⟺ 8p+1 is a norm from ℤ[√2] with NOT all factors ≡ 1 mod 8. Is 8p+1 always a norm from ℤ[√2]? No — need (2/q) = 1 for all q ∥ 8p+1 to odd power... So the C=2 analysis splits: either 8p+1 has a prime factor ≡ 3,5 mod 8 — then that factor is not ≡ −1 mod 8 and doesn't directly certify, but a product of a ≡ 3 and a ≡ 5 factor is ≡ 15 ≡ 7 ✓ certifies! So C = 2 wins iff the prime factors of 8p+1 (mod 8) admit a subset product ≡ 7 — i.e. NOT(all factors ≡ 1) AND NOT(all non-1 factors are in a single class {3} or {5} with... ) — exactly the subset-product condition. Enumerate the failure patterns mod 8.
why: For C ≤ 3 the failure conditions are fully explicit finite patterns on the multiset of prime residues; listing them exactly is the base case for the 'failure taxonomy' and for a potential 'C ≤ K failure ⟹ contradiction' argument.
first_step: For C = 1, 2, 3, 4, 6: list the exact failure patterns on multisets of prime residues mod 4C; compute densities; verify against data.

title: Joint failure for C = 1 and C = 2: p with 4p+1 all factors ≡ 1 mod 4 AND 8p+1 failing the mod-8 pattern — a two-condition sieve whose density and *correlation* are computable

Independence of the two factorisations is the sieve heuristic; the actual joint density vs the product of marginals quantifies the correlation (via p's residues mod small primes which affect both).
why: If the joint failure density factorises (independence holds to good accuracy), the heuristic exp(−Σ) stands; the correlation structure at small C is where any 'conspiracy' enabling a counterexample would show up.
first_step: Compute the joint and marginal failure frequencies for C ∈ {1,2,3,4,6} over p ≤ 10⁷; compute all pairwise correlations.

title: QNR condition for full Type II: is (f/p) forced for ff′ = 4c²dp + 1 with f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 (mod 4cd)?
connection: Repeat the C-form derivation: 4c²dp ≡ −1 (mod f) ⟹ (c²dp/f)(−1)... (4c²dp/f) = (dp/f) = (−1/f) = −1 since f ≡ 3 mod 4. And (d/f) by reciprocity with f ≡ −1 mod 4d: (d/f) = +1 (same computation as for C). So (p/f) = −1 again, i.e. (f/p) = −1: every Type II certificate factor is a QNR mod p. Check also Type I: f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p mod 4cd — here p² ≡ −4c²d mod f, so (−d/f) = +1 is forced instead (a condition on f, not on p).
why: Extends the lemma to all of Type II (so T1 for Type II is the same two-line argument), and shows Type I has a DIFFERENT forced symbol ((−d/f) = 1, i.e. f splits in ℚ(√−d)) — the two types have structurally different reciprocity signatures, which may be why both are needed.
first_step: Verify numerically for p < 3000: (f/p) = −1 for all Type II certificates; (−d/f) = 1 for all Type I certificates; then check whether Type I has any forced symbol involving p (e.g. (f/p) given f ≡ −p mod 4cd: (f/p) = (−p mod stuff…) — compute empirically the distribution of (f/p) over Type I certificates).

title: Exceptional primes 409, 577, 5569, 9601: search for a second forced symbol via the 2-adic structure of a
connection: For C even (8 | 4C) we need a ≡ −1 mod 8; for C odd a ≡ 3 mod 4 only. The QNR condition (a/p) = −1 plus a ≡ −1 (mod 4C) plus a | 4Cp + 1. For p ≡ 1 mod 8 (577, 5569, 9601): (2/p) = 1 so the 2-part of a is irrelevant to (a/p)… The obstruction (if any) must come from the interplay of a mod 4C and a mod p via a | 4Cp+1: a ≡ −1 mod 4C and 4Cp ≡ −1 mod a. Consider the Jacobi symbol (a / (4Cp+1)/a) = (a/b): since a ≡ b ≡ −1 mod 4 … (a/b)(b/a) = −1 (both ≡ 3 mod 4); and (b/a) = (4Cp+1)/a … b ≡ (4Cp+1)/a; 4Cp+1 ≡ 1 mod a? No: a | 4Cp+1 so 4Cp+1 ≡ 0 mod a; b = (4Cp+1)/a, (b/a) = ? not determined. Hmm. Try instead a mod p: a·b ≡ 1 mod p, a ≡ b ≡ −1 mod 4C: a + b ≡ −2 mod 4C and ab = 4Cp + 1: so (a + b + 2) ≡ 0 mod 4C and (a+1)(b+1) = ab + a + b + 1 = 4Cp + a + b + 2 ≡ 0 mod 4C — consistent. The pair (a, b) are roots of t² − s t + (4Cp+1) with s = a + b ≡ −2 mod 4C: discriminant s² − 4(4Cp+1) = (a − b)² must be a square. So C-form certificate ⟺ ∃ s ≡ −2 (mod 4C): s² − 16Cp − 4 is a perfect square ⟺ (s/2)² − 4Cp − 1 = (r)² with s/2 ≡ −1 mod 2C: ⟺ 4Cp + 1 = σ² − r² with σ ≡ −1 (mod 2C). So: C-form ⟺ 4Cp + 1 is a difference of two squares σ² − r² with σ ≡ −1 mod 2C (automatically σ ± r ≡ −1 mod 4C? need check). This 'difference of squares with a congruence' form is a new angle on the exceptions.
why: The 'σ² − r² with σ ≡ −1 mod 2C' form is a quadratic condition in two variables (σ, r) — suitable for genus/local analysis at the exceptional primes: for which p is σ² − r² = 4Cp + 1, σ ≡ −1 (2C) locally solvable for all C but globally never? Local solvability is presumably automatic; the exceptions would then be 'non-BM integral Hasse failures' of a FAMILY of conics — which is exactly the kind of phenomenon the Bright–Loughran framework studies.
first_step: Verify the equivalence (σ² − r² = 4Cp+1, σ ≡ −1 mod 2C ⟺ C-form certificate) numerically; then for p = 409, run the local analysis: for each C, is there a local obstruction (mod powers of 2, mod primes dividing C) to σ² − r² = 4·409·C + 1 with σ ≡ −1 mod 2C? If always locally solvable, the exceptions are integral Hasse failures — report.
