first_step: Compute for all primes ≡ 1 mod 24 below 20000 the invariants (x, y with p = x² + y², v₂(y), h(−4p) mod 16, quartic character of 2, p mod 48/96) and find any invariant that separates the four exceptions from the rest.

title: Additive combinatorics: the set of C-form certificates for fixed p as a 'multiplicative energy' problem on divisors of {4Cp+1}_C
connection: Writing 4Cp + 1 = ab with a + 1 ≡ b + 1 ≡ 0 (mod 4C): the condition says 4C | gcd(a+1, b+1) and 4C = (ab − 1)/p. So C-form certificates ⟺ pairs (a, b) with (ab − 1)/p dividing both a + 1 and b + 1, and ab ≡ 1 mod p. The set {(a,b): ab ≡ 1 mod p} is the modular hyperbola; we need points on it where the 'height' (ab−1)/p divides a + 1. For a, b ≤ p this forces (ab − 1)/p < p; so it's a question about the modular hyperbola's small-height points with a divisibility — a sum-product-flavoured condition.
why: Sum-product/energy methods (Bourgain–Garaev on modular hyperbolas, Shkredov) give nontrivial pointwise-in-p bounds for incidence-type counts on the hyperbola; they could show the count of (a, b) with the divisibility is ≫ 1 for all p? Unlikely (counts are small) but the hyperbola geometry is the right home for 'why 409 fails'.
first_step: Plot, for p = 409 and a control prime 401, the points (a, b) with ab ≡ 1 mod p, a, b < 4p, colouring those with (ab − 1)/p | gcd(a+1, b+1); see the structural difference.

title: Hilbert's tenth problem / Diophantine-set lens: the ES solution set {(n, x, y, z)} is Diophantine; the set of 'good n' is a projection — is it a 'universal' Diophantine set or a very simple one?
connection: All r.e. sets are Diophantine (MRDP), but ES's good set is conjecturally everything ≥ 2; the *complexity* (number of variables/degree) of the simplest Diophantine representation of 'n has no solution' (if ES is false, that set is nonempty) — a negative Diophantine definition requires bounding x, y, z: 'for all x,y,z ≤ B(n), 4xyz ≠ n(xy+yz+zx)', expressible with bounded universal quantifiers (Davis normal form). Curiosity: which small Diophantine sets contain all primes ≡ 1 mod 24? (Jones–Sato–Wada–Wiens prime polynomial…)
why: Pure logic-flavoured calibration; low value but cheap to note.
first_step: Note; skip unless a logician collaborator is interested.

title: abc-conjecture consequences: does abc bound the size of the smallest certificate or forbid 'all 4Cp+1 nearly prime for C ≤ K'?
connection: abc gives bounds on smooth/powerful values of polynomials; the 'hard prime' heuristic requires 4Cp+1 to be nearly prime (few factors) for all small C — not an abc-type condition. But abc does bound solutions of, e.g., 4Cp + 1 = a·b with a, b both powerful; not relevant. Mostly a negative: abc is about radicals, ES about residues. Keep as a 5-minute check.
why: Rule out quickly; conditional abc results are popular and someone will ask.
first_step: Write one paragraph: why abc (radical-based) is orthogonal to residue-class divisor conditions; note any exception (e.g. Granville's 'abc ⟹ squarefree values of polynomials' would make 4Cp+1 squarefree often — mild help for the subset-product counting).
refs: Granville, 'ABC allows us to count squarefrees' (1998)

title: Catalan/Mihăilescu-style cyclotomic rigidity for 'ab = 4Cp+1, a + 1 ≡ b + 1 ≡ 0 mod 4C': a Wieferich-type congruence?
connection: Mihăilescu's proof of Catalan used Wieferich-type pairs (p^{q−1} ≡ 1 mod q²) derived from cyclotomic unit structure. The ES C-form has the structure ab ≡ 1 (mod p) with a ≡ b ≡ −1 (mod 4C) and 4C | (ab − 1)/p... Any 'double congruence' (mod p and mod 4C simultaneously, with 4C | ab − 1 too) resembles Wieferich conditions. Check: is ab ≡ 1 mod 4Cp? ab = 4Cp + 1 ≡ 1 mod 4Cp — yes trivially. And a ≡ −1 mod 4C ⟹ a^2 ≡ 1 mod 4C... So a² ≡ 1 (mod 4C) and ab ≡ 1 (mod 4C) ⟹ b ≡ a mod 4C ✓. Nothing deep; drop unless a cyclotomic-unit argument appears.
why: Low; included for completeness of the 'rigidity mechanisms' sweep.
first_step: Drop after noting.

title: Tool: use Pari/GP's `factor` with `factorint` flags (ECM) to push the C-form census to p ≤ 10⁷ and C ≤ 10⁴ cheaply; publish the exceptional list to OEIS
connection: The C-form exceptional primes (409, 577, 5569, 9601, …) form a natural integer sequence not (apparently) in OEIS; computing it to 10⁷ and submitting it creates a public hook for others.
why: Community/visibility item with a concrete deliverable; OEIS entries attract exactly the kind of elementary-number-theory attention that could explain the exceptions.
first_step: Run the census (Pari, ~hours); check OEIS for the sequence; draft an OEIS submission with the definition 'primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4) with no C ≤ 10⁴ such that 4Cp+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C'.

title: Count the C-form exceptional primes up to X: density → 0 like 1/(log X)^α? or positive density?
connection: If exceptions have positive relative density among primes ≡ 1 mod 24, the C-form is a 'weak' sufficient condition; if they thin out as a power of log, they are the 'tail' and their rate is a measurable analogue of exceptional-set exponents (Vaughan's bound in miniature).
why: Quantifies the gap between C-form and ES; also a test of the 'half-dimensional sieve' heuristics (prediction: exceptions ~ X/(log X)^{1+κ} for the effective sieve dimension κ).
first_step: From the census, fit #exceptions ≤ X vs X/(log X)^β; report β.

title: Which composites fail the C-form? Test whether C-form exceptions are closed under multiplication by squares or by other exceptions
connection: If n fails the C-form, does n·m² fail? (T1-like scaling: for squares the obstruction is via (a/m²) = 1; for n·m²: (a/nm²) = (a/n) — so the QNR condition reduces to that of n; and 4C·nm² + 1 = ab with a ≡ −1 (4C) — different integer.) Empirically test closure properties of the exceptional set E = {n : no C-form certificate}.
why: Structural properties of E (closure, multiplicativity) constrain any eventual characterisation; e.g. if E ⊇ {odd squares} ∪ {409 m² : m odd}, there are infinite non-square families, changing the 'squares + sporadic' expectation for this sub-conjecture.

title: Analogy: Lehmer's totient problem / 'Giuga numbers' — sets defined by 'all prime factors satisfy a congruence' are provably thin and structured; the C-form failure set is such a set for each C
connection: For C = 1: 4p + 1 ∈ S₁ := {all prime factors ≡ 1 mod 4} — the 'sum of two squares' type set. For general C: 4Cp+1 ∈ S_C := {subset products of prime factors avoid −1 mod 4C}. Each S_C is a 'multiplicatively defined' set with a Landau-type counting function x/(log x)^{1−δ_C}; the failure set is {p : ∀C, 4Cp + 1 ∈ S_C}. Sets of the form {n : ∀C ≤ K, aC n + b ∈ S_C} are 'simultaneous Landau conditions on linear forms' — a sieve-theoretic object with a known theory for FIXED K (Brun–Hooley), and the uniformity in K is the frontier.
why: Names the problem as a 'simultaneous multiplicative-set membership of linear forms', connecting to the Hooley 'applications of sieve methods' chapter on sums of two squares in APs/linear forms.
first_step: Read Hooley, Applications of Sieve Methods ch. 5 (two squares in linear forms); formulate the K-fold version; check what uniformity in K the method allows.
refs: Hooley, Applications of Sieve Methods to the Theory of Numbers (1976)

title: Analogy: 'primes p such that p + 1 is a sum of two squares' (Iwaniec) — the half-dimensional sieve as the exact tool for 'C = 1 fails'
connection: C = 1 fails ⟺ 4p+1 has all prime factors ≡ 1 mod 4 ⟺ 4p+1 is 'primitively' a sum of two squares with no factor ≡ 3 mod 4 — the half-dimensional sieve's territory (Iwaniec 1972: #{p ≤ x: p + 1 = a² + b²} ≍ x/(log x)^{3/2}). So #{p ≤ x: C=1 fails} ≍ x/(log x)^{3/2}: a THEOREM-level statement (upper AND lower bounds) about the simplest failure set.
why: Gives the first rigorous 'failure-set size' at C = 1 with matching lower bound — a template for C ≤ K failure sets and a sanity anchor for all heuristics (the constant can be compared with data).
first_step: Check Iwaniec's theorem applies to 4p+1 (linear form in p with leading coefficient 4; yes, 'Primes of the type φ(x,y) + A'/'half-dimensional sieve' handle p + A; for 4p + 1 check the admissibility); compute the constant and compare with the empirical count up to 10⁷.
refs: Iwaniec, 'Primes of the type φ(x,y)+A where φ is a quadratic form', Acta Arith 21 (1972)

title: Upper-bound sieve on simultaneous failure for C ∈ {1, 2}: #{p ≤ x : 4p+1 ∈ S₁ and 8p+1 ∈ S₂} ≪ x/(log x)^{1+1/2+δ₂}
connection: Each extra C with an index-2-type failure set adds 1/2 to the sieve dimension; S₂ (mod 8 patterns) has 'dimension' depending on which residue classes mod 8 are excluded from the subset-product condition (computed via the failure patterns). A K-fold simultaneous Landau sieve with dimension κ_K = Σ_C δ_C and explicit constants.
why: For fixed K this is a theorem-level upper bound; the K → ∞ uniformity gives exceptional-set bounds; and comparing with data at K = 2, 3 is a precise calibration of sieve constants vs reality.
first_step: Compute δ_C (the density exponent of S_C) for C ≤ 6 from the failure patterns; run a Selberg sieve numerically for K = 2 to get the constant; compare with the empirical joint-failure count to 10⁷.

title: The subset-product failure set S_C has a 'dimension' δ_C = 1 − (fraction of residue classes that can contribute): compute δ_C for all C ≤ 100 and its asymptotics
connection: For S_C defined by 'subset products of prime factors (mod 4C) avoid −1', a first-order density exponent is obtained by the largest −1-free subgroup H ⊂ (ℤ/4C)^× (density of primes in H = |H|/φ(4C)); 'all factors in H' has counting function x/(log x)^{1 − |H|/φ(4C)}. The maximal −1-free subgroup has index 2 (any subgroup not containing −1 can be enlarged to index 2? Not always: in (ℤ/8)^× = {1,3,5,7}, −1 = 7; −1-free subgroups: {1}, {1,3}, {1,5} — index 2 exist ✓. In general, −1 ∉ H means H ∩ ⟨−1⟩ trivial; H can be extended to a complement of ⟨−1⟩ if the group is... (ℤ/4C)^× ≅ ℤ/2 × stuff; −1 may or may not be a 'direct summand' — e.g. in ℤ/4 (cyclic), −1 = 2 is the unique element of order 2, every nontrivial subgroup contains it! So for (ℤ/4C)^× containing a cyclic ℤ/4 summand in which −1 lies... concretely for 4C = 20: (ℤ/20)^× ≅ ℤ/2 × ℤ/4 with −1 = ? ; the −1-free subgroups may have index 4.) So δ_C varies non-trivially with C — compute it.
why: δ_C controls how 'hard' it is for a prime to fail at C: small δ_C (large −1-free subgroup) = easy to fail; the C with largest δ_C are the most 'useful' certificates; a proof would use them. Possibly δ_C → 1 along C with (ℤ/4C)^× having −1 'deeply embedded' (e.g. 4C = 4q with q ≡ 1 mod 4 prime? then (ℤ/4q)^× ≅ ℤ/2 × ℤ/(q−1), −1 = (1, (q−1)/2); −1-free subgroups can have index 2: take {0} × ℤ/(q−1)? contains (0,(q−1)/2) ≠ −1 = (1, (q−1)/2) ✓ index 2. Hmm so index 2 always possible? Need −1 ∉ some index-2 subgroup ⟺ −1 is not a square… ⟺ some character χ mod 4C with χ(−1) = −1 (odd character) — ALWAYS exists for 4C ≥ 3. So index-2 −1-free subgroups always exist: δ_C ≤ 1/2 for all C.) So every C has δ_C = 1/2 at the top level — failure at C costs exactly (log)^{-1/2}·(const_C). Then the heuristic failure density for all C ≤ K is (log p)^{−K/2}·Π const_C, where const_C encodes the finer structure. Verify.
first_step: For C ≤ 100: list all −1-free subgroups, their indices; confirm index 2 always achievable; compute the full generating-function density of S_C (sum over all failure patterns, not just 'all in H') numerically for 4Cp+1 ≤ 10⁷.

title: ES as 'every p has an odd character χ mod 4C and a divisor a of 4Cp+1 with χ(a) = −1 for ALL odd χ' — the character-theoretic restatement of a ≡ −1 (mod 4C)
connection: a ≡ −1 mod 4C ⟺ χ(a) = χ(−1) for all characters χ mod 4C ⟺ χ(a) = −1 for odd χ and +1 for even χ. So the C-form asks for a divisor whose character vector equals that of −1. The 'subgroup relaxation' keeps only one odd character; the full condition is ALL characters. Framing: find (C, a) with χ(a) = χ(−1) ∀χ — a 'complete set of character conditions', the number of which grows with C (φ(4C) conditions), while the number of divisors grows like τ(4Cp+1) ≈ log p on average — the expected number of hits is τ/φ(4C), and Σ_C τ(4Cp+1)/φ(4C) ≈ log p · Σ 1/C → log p · log X. (Same count as before, now seen as 'characters vs divisors'.)
why: The character view suggests a *Fourier-analytic* route: #certificates at C = (1/φ(4C)) Σ_χ χ(−1) Σ_{a | N} χ(a); the χ = trivial term is τ(N)/φ(4C) > 0; the other terms are 'noise' Σ_{a|N} χ(a) = Π_{q^e ∥ N} (1 + χ(q) + … + χ(q)^e). A certificate fails to exist iff the noise exactly cancels the main term. Average over C of the noise — can it be shown to be o(main) at fixed p? That's the M_BM program (B3 says the average main term is only log²p). Record the restatement.
first_step: Write the exact identity and compute, for p = 409 and C ≤ 1000, main vs noise per C to see HOW cancellation happens (is it via single-prime N = q with χ(q) = +1 for all odd χ — i.e. q ≡ 1-type — or via multi-factor cancellations?).

title: For p = 409, tabulate the factorisation type of 4Cp+1 for C ≤ 1000: how does 'no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C' happen each time (prime? all factors ≡ 1 mod 4C? subgroup?)
connection: Direct forensic analysis of the exception: a histogram of failure reasons for one prime across C.
why: If the failures are 'random-looking' (mixture of reasons), 409 is a statistical accident and larger C must win (contradicting the C ≤ 60000 search — making an obstruction likely); if a single reason dominates (e.g. all factors always in a particular subgroup), the obstruction is visible.
first_step: Compute and classify; compare with a control prime (401 or 433) where the C-form wins quickly.

title: Could the C-form exceptional set be 'odd squares ∪ {p : (2/p)… something} ∪ finite' with the exceptions explained by a *quartic* reciprocity law?
connection: HKRS's Apollonian obstructions include quartic ones; the C-form's forced (a/p) = −1 is quadratic. A quartic analogue would be: when p ≡ 1 mod 8 and ... the quartic symbol (a/p)_4 is forced to a value that contradicts (a/p) = −1. For p ≡ 1 mod 8 (577, 5569, 9601 all ≡ 1 mod 8!; 409 ≡ 1 mod 8 too: 409 = 408 + 1 = 8·51 + 1 ✓). All four exceptions are ≡ 1 mod 8 — consistent with a quartic (mod 8-sensitive) obstruction acting on a subset of the p ≡ 1 mod 8 primes. Most primes ≡ 1 mod 8 do have certificates, so the obstruction would need another condition (e.g. 2 is a quartic residue, p = x² + 64y²).
why: Concrete, testable hypothesis class for the exceptions.
first_step: Compute for the four exceptions whether 2 is a quartic residue (p = x² + 64y²?) and whether −1 is an octic residue (p ≡ 1 mod 16?); compare to the frequency of these among non-exceptional primes ≡ 1 mod 8 below 20000.

title: Mechanism design: an identity family indexed by the Gaussian factorisation p = u² + v² (not polynomial in p but polynomial in (u, v))
connection: Mordell–Schinzel forbids polynomial identities in p on square classes; identities polynomial in (u, v) with p = u² + v² are a different class (p is a quadratic form in the parameters). E.g. try: 4/(u² + v²) = 1/x(u,v) + 1/y(u,v) + 1/z(u,v) with x, y, z ∈ ℤ[u, v] — a polynomial identity in TWO variables over the quadric. Schinzel's theorem is about one variable n; a two-variable identity covering all (u, v) with u² + v² ≡ 1 mod 24 is not obviously excluded (but a polynomial identity in (u,v) specialises to a polynomial identity in n on... no — n = u² + v² does not make x(u,v) a polynomial in n). Also allowed: identities depending on (u, v) mod small moduli.
why: A genuinely different identity class that respects T1 automatically? (Odd squares m² = u² + v² with... m² = (m)² + 0² or other representations; identities valid only for v ≠ 0 or for gcd(u,v) = 1 would exclude the trivial representation — promising sign.) Search space is small; cheap to run.
first_step: Enumerate candidate x, y, z as low-degree polynomials in (u, v) (degree ≤ 4, small coefficients) satisfying 4xyz = (u²+v²)(xy+yz+zx) identically — polynomial system; solve with Gröbner/ansatz; also allow residue-class branching on (u, v) mod 2, 3, 4.

title: Identity families indexed by other binary forms representing p: p = u² + 2v², u² + 3v², u² − 2v², u² + uv + v²
connection: Every p ≡ 1 mod 24 is simultaneously u² + v², u² + 2v² (p ≡ 1,3 mod 8 ✓), u² + 3v² (p ≡ 1 mod 3 ✓), u² − 2v² (p ≡ ±1 mod 8 ✓), u² + 6v²? (needs p ≡ 1, 7 mod 24 ✓!). Each representation gives 2 parameters; polynomial identities in those parameters are not excluded by Mordell–Schinzel.
why: Multiplies the search space of 'legal' identity classes by the number of forms; the combination 'p = u² + 6v²' is special to the hard class p ≡ 1 mod 24.
first_step: Same Gröbner/ansatz search for each form; for p = u² + 6v² in particular (since 24 | 840 structure).
refs: Cox, Primes of the form x² + ny²

title: Does T1 kill (u, v)-identities? Check what happens to a (u,v)-polynomial identity at p = m² = u² + v²
connection: If an identity in (u,v) valid for all coprime (u,v) with u² + v² ≡ 1 mod 24 existed, it would produce Type I/II solutions for m² whenever m² = u² + v² with gcd(u,v) = 1 and uv ≠ 0 — which happens iff m has a prime factor ≡ 1 mod 4 (Pythagorean). T1 says no such solution exists ⟹ NO (u,v)-polynomial identity can be valid on all coprime (u,v) with the right residues. So (u,v)-identities must also exclude Pythagorean (u,v) — i.e. must depend on more than residues of (u,v). Record as a lemma killing the naive version; the surviving version needs a non-polynomial ingredient (e.g. gcd or primality of u² + v²).
why: Saves a wasted search; and pinpoints the 'Pythagorean' loophole: an identity could be valid only when u² + v² is not a square — but polynomial identities can't 'know' that. Same for u² + 2v², etc. (m² = u² + 2v² has solutions when m has a factor ≡ 1,3 mod 8).
first_step: Write the lemma; then ask: are there identities in (u,v) valid for all (u,v) with u² + v² ≡ 1 mod 24 EXCEPT where u² + v² is a square — impossible for polynomials; so the item above (Gaussian identities) is dead in its polynomial form; keep only residue-branching + non-polynomial variants.

title: Analogy of analogy: T1 ↔ 'Pythagorean loophole' ↔ Hilbert's irreducibility — identities fail exactly where the parameter polynomial takes square values; so ES's obstruction is the square-value locus of EVERY parametrisation
connection: Generalising the previous item: for any parametrisation p = P(t₁, …, t_k) (P a polynomial), a polynomial identity would produce solutions at all values P(t) including those that are odd squares; T1 forbids this; so no polynomial identity exists over any parametrisation P whose value set contains odd squares. Only parametrisations whose value set avoids squares (e.g. P(t) = t² + 1, never a square for t ≥ 1; P = 4t² + 1 never a square for t ≥ 1!) escape. So: polynomial identities for ES along p = 4t² + 1 (or t² + 1, t⁴ + 1…) are NOT excluded by T1 — and primes of the form 4t² + 1 are conjecturally infinite (Landau's 4th problem for t²+1).
why: Identifies a precise loophole class: identities in t for n = 4t² + 1 (or similar square-avoiding polynomials) — a 'conditional infinite family of hard primes' if found (hard class? 4t² + 1 mod 840 can be in square classes: need 4t² + 1 ≡ square mod 840 for some t ✓ possible). Mordell–Schinzel applies to identities in n, not in t with n = 4t² + 1 — check Schinzel's theorem's exact scope (it might cover 'polynomial in t with n polynomial in t').
first_step: Search for polynomial x(t), y(t), z(t) with 4/(4t² + 1) = Σ 1/x_i(t); e.g. try the e-slice/Type II structure: 4C(4t² + 1) + 1 = 16Ct² + 4C + 1 — for C = 1: 16t² + 5 — factor? no; find C(t) polynomial making 4C(t)(4t² + 1) + 1 factor with the right residues. Then read Schinzel 2000 to see whether this is excluded.

title: ES for n = t² + 1 and n = 4t² + 1: compute identities and check whether the campaign already knows 'ES holds for all n = t² + 1'
connection: n = t² + 1: 4/(t²+1) — try x = (t²+1)/… hmm t² + 1 ≡ 1,2 mod 4; for t even n ≡ 1 mod 4. Is there a known identity? e.g. 4/(t²+1) = 1/(t²+1)·4; want 1/A + 1/B + 1/C. Note (t² + 1) + t² ... Possibly known in the literature on 'Erdős–Straus for n = polynomial values' (e.g. 'all n of the form k² + 1'?). Search.
why: If identities exist for square-avoiding polynomial families, that's an infinite family of hard-class n (not primes necessarily) — and the proof technique (polynomial in t) shows how T1 is dodged; worth 30 minutes.
first_step: git grep -il 't^2+1\|t² + 1\|k^2+1' -- '*.md'; brute-force search for identities with x, y, z ∈ ℤ[t] of degree ≤ 4 for n = t² + 1, 4t² + 1, t² + t + 1.

title: Geometry: integral points on the surface 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) as n varies — the threefold X: 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) in (x,y,z,n) and its fibration over n; is X rational? unirational? what are its integral points' densities?
connection: The total space X ⊂ A⁴ is a cubic threefold (linear in n!): n = 4xyz/(xy+yz+zx) — so X ≅ the graph of a rational function on A³: X is rational, integral points = (x,y,z) with (xy+yz+zx) | 4xyz. ES = surjectivity of n: ℤ³_{>0} ∩ X → ℤ_{≥2}. The question 'which integers are values of 4xyz/(xy+yz+zx)' is a 'value set of a rational function at integer points' problem.
why: Reframes ES as the image of an explicit rational map on integer points — related to the theory of 'representation by rational functions' and to Heath-Brown-style counts of integer points on cubic hypersurfaces where the count of points with a given value of n is f(n). The threefold's geometry (it's rational, the fibres are the U_n) gives a 'total count' Σ_{n ≤ N} f(n) via lattice points on X, which is the Elsholtz–Tao estimate; nothing new, but the 'value set of a rational function' literature (e.g. values of x/y + y/z + z/x) might have transferable ideas.
first_step: Search 'integers of the form 4xyz/(xy+yz+zx)' and the similar classical 'x/y + y/z + z/x = n' problem (Bremner–Guy; elliptic curves!): the latter is an elliptic surface where integer values are determined by rank — a structurally different (and solvable) situation. Compare: why does xy+yz+zx | 4xyz NOT reduce to elliptic curves?

title: Compare ES with x/y + y/z + z/x = n (Bremner–Guy): both are 'n as a value of a symmetric rational function in 3 variables'; the latter reduces to elliptic curves with rank-dependent solvability — what makes ES's function (harmonic mean) different?
connection: 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z says n/4 is... the harmonic mean of x,y,z divided by 3: HM/3·… ; x/y + y/z + z/x = n defines a cubic curve in P² for each n (genus 1); 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) is a cubic surface (dimension 2) — more freedom, hence many solutions (log²n) rather than rank-controlled finitely many. So ES is 'easier' in count but lacks the group law. A middle ground: intersect U_n with a plane (e.g. z = x + y or z = kx) to get a curve; integer points on these curves (genus 0 or 1) — for genus 0 fibres (lines/conics), integral points are governed by Pell/congruence conditions — these are the identity families; are there genus-1 plane sections with positive rank for all n? Then infinitely many rational points — but integrality is the catch.
why: Systematises 'plane sections of U_n' as the source of all known identities (genus 0 sections) and asks whether genus-1 sections offer anything (they give rational, not integral, points — usually useless for ES, but integral points on elliptic curves are a finite set with effective bounds, so 'every n has an integral point on some genus-1 section' is at least a well-posed hard problem).
first_step: Classify plane sections of U_n by genus; list which genus-0 sections give Mordell's identities; find a genus-1 section family and compute its rank for small n (Sage) for curiosity.

title: Community: write up the C-form exceptional primes + QNR lemma as a short arXiv note / MO question to invite elementary explanations
connection: The observations (C-form strictly weaker than ES; four exceptional primes below 20000 with no certificate to C = 60000; every certificate divisor is a QNR mod p) are elementary and crisp — ideal for an MO question 'Why does 409 have no factorisation 4C·409 + 1 = ab with a ≡ b ≡ −1 mod 4C?'
why: Crowd-sourced elementary number theory is strong at exactly this kind of question; a quick answer would either kill a sub-conjecture (local obstruction) or reveal a mechanism.
first_step: Verify the four exceptions independently (Pari), extend to 10⁶ for the list, then post on MO with the QNR lemma.

title: Sanity: does the C-form exceptional set change if we also allow a ≡ −1 (mod 4C) with a | 4Cp − 1 (sign variant) or 4Cp + 1 = ab with a ≡ b ≡ +1 (mod 4C)? Which sign variants correspond to actual ES solutions?
connection: The derivation p = 4Cuv − u − v gave the (−1, −1) sign pattern; ES's word form allows a coordinate in (8ℤ − p) too — other sign/parity patterns may correspond to Type I. Enumerate all 'sign variants' of the C-form, determine which yield ES solutions (verify algebraically), and recompute the exceptional set under the union.
why: The exceptional primes might simply be certified by a sibling form (e.g. Type I with c = 1), which would make 'C-form exceptions' a statement about one sign pattern only — important for interpreting the finding.
first_step: Derive: 4/p = 1/(Cuv) + 1/(pCv) + 1/(pCu) came from p + u + v = 4Cuv; alternatives: p + u − v = 4Cuv? (gives a negative term?) ; p − u − v = 4Cuv ⟹ 4/p = ... check signs; list all variants giving positive solutions; compute which certify 409.

title: Type I at c = 1 ('f | p² + 4d, f ≡ −p mod 4d'): the Type-I sibling of the C-form — which primes does IT certify, and does it cover 409, 577, 5569, 9601?
connection: The one-parameter Type I family (c = 1) is the natural sibling; its certificates are divisors of p² + 4d in class −p mod 4d. Compute its exceptional set and the intersection with the C-form exceptional set; ES holds for all four exceptions (they have c=2 Type II), but do they have c=1 Type I?
why: Determines whether 'one-parameter' forms (c = 1 of either type) suffice empirically, or whether the two-parameter slack is essential for some primes — a structural fact about ES's 'dimension'.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 20000 the c=1 Type I certificate existence (d ≤ 10⁴); list exceptions; intersect with the C-form exceptions.

title: Minimal 'dimension' of ES: is there a one-parameter family of certificates (any type) covering all primes ≤ 10⁷?
connection: The C-form (Type II, c=1) fails for some primes; Type I with c=1 may fail for others; their union might cover everything — or might not, implying that ES is intrinsically 'two-parameter' (any one-parameter sub-family has exceptions). That would be a quantitative version of 'no covering by identities': even infinite one-parameter families don't suffice.
why: A sharp structural fact about ES, cheap to establish empirically, with implications for proof design (must handle two-parameter families → double sums → the extra log).
first_step: Compute exceptional sets of: C-form; c=1 Type I; e-slice with e ≤ bound (one parameter: e); and their union, for p ≤ 10⁶.

title: Physics redux: the C-form as a 1-D 'Ising chain in a field' where the field is the character χ and the spins are prime factors — exact solvability (transfer matrix) of the per-C partition function
connection: #{a | N: a ≡ −1 (4C)} = (1/φ) Σ_χ χ(−1) Π_{q^e ∥ N} (1 + χ(q) + … + χ(q)^e) is literally a sum over 'external fields' χ of a product of single-site partition functions — an exactly solvable (non-interacting) model. ES failure = destructive interference across χ. The physics intuition: non-interacting spins in φ(4C) different fields; the total vanishes iff … This is exactly the structure where 'Lee–Yang' and 'sign problem' intuitions apply: the sum over χ is a sum with signs (χ(−1) = ±1 and complex χ(q)).
why: Just the exact formula in physics clothing; but the 'sign problem' analogy suggests looking at |Σ| vs Σ|·| — the ratio measures cancellation; and the structure 'product of single-site terms' means the count is a *Fourier transform of a product* — a convolution on the group, which is where Kneser/subset-sum structure enters (item on additive combinatorics).
first_step: Compute the cancellation ratio (count)/(Σ_χ |Π|)/φ for failing vs winning (p, C); see whether failures are 'maximal cancellation' events with a recognisable pattern.

title: Convolution-on-group view: the divisor multiset of N mod 4C is a multiset D ⊂ (ℤ/4C)^×; certificates = D ∋ −1; D = product-set of the prime-power 'intervals' {1, q, …, q^e} — a Minkowski product of 'geometric progressions' in the group; Kneser's theorem bounds |D| from below
connection: |D| ≥ Σ (|D_q| − 1) + 1 (Cauchy–Davenport analogue for abelian groups via Kneser) when there is no stabiliser; so with ω(N) factors, |D| ≥ ω + 1 roughly — tiny versus φ(4C). Kneser's theorem also says: if |D| is small then D is a union of cosets of a subgroup H (periodic) — then −1 ∈ D iff the coset structure includes it: a *structural* dichotomy: either D is large (random-like, then −1 ∈ D with 'probability' |D|/φ) or D is periodic with stabiliser H (then −1 ∈ D ⟺ −1 ∈ D·H, a subgroup question). This is a rigorous version of the 'subgroup vs subset-product' gap.
why: Kneser's structure theorem is a real theorem applicable pointwise (at each (p, C)); it reorganises failures into 'small non-periodic D' (few factors — the dominant failure mode) vs 'periodic D missing −1' (subgroup obstruction).
first_step: For (p, C) failures, compute D, its stabiliser H = {h : hD = D}, and classify; check the Kneser bound tightness.

title: Ask: is there any (p, C) failure with ω(4Cp+1) ≥ 6 where D is NOT a union of cosets of a nontrivial subgroup? (Kneser-periodicity test of 'rich' failures)
connection: If rich failures (many prime factors) are always periodic (D = union of H-cosets with H ∌ −1 and H nontrivial), then failures split cleanly into 'poor' (ω ≤ 5) and 'periodic'. The periodic ones are controlled by Galois (all factors in a subgroup); the poor ones by sieve (few prime factors is rare across C). A proof could treat the two regimes separately.
why: Sharp empirical dichotomy test with direct proof-strategy consequences.
first_step: Scan p ≤ 10⁵, C ≤ 200 for failures with ω ≥ 6; compute stabilisers.

title: Sieve for 'poor' failures: #{C ≤ X : ω(4Cp+1) ≤ 5} ≪ X (log log X)⁵/log X — pointwise in p by an upper-bound sieve (Hardy–Ramanujan / Brun) — so most C have rich 4Cp+1
connection: Upper-bound sieves bound the number of C ≤ X for which the linear form 4Cp+1 has few prime factors (almost-prime values of a linear polynomial): ≪ X/log X · (log log X)^k uniformly in p ≤ X^A? (Need uniformity in the coefficient 4p: standard sieve bounds for almost-primes in APs are uniform via Brun–Titchmarsh-type results, with p up to X^{1−ε}... For X = polylog(p) the uniformity fails — the coefficient 4p is huge relative to X. Hmm: the sieve dimension is 1, the sifting range is primes ≤ z; for values 4Cp+1 ≤ 4Xp, we sieve by primes up to z ≈ X^{1/2}: the count of C ≤ X with 4Cp+1 free of primes ≤ z is ≪ X/log z — that's fine and uniform in p (only the residue of p mod q matters). So #{C ≤ X: 4Cp+1 has no prime factor ≤ X^{1/2}} ≪ X/log X — pointwise in p! But 'rich' needs ≥ 6 factors, not just one small factor.) Refine: with k-fold sieving (Erdős–Kac-type for linear forms, Halberstam) one gets most C have ω(4Cp+1) ≈ log log(Xp)… uniformity in p needs the Turán–Kubilius inequality for linear forms with large coefficient — it holds! (The variance Σ_C (ω(4Cp+1) − log log)² ≪ X log log, uniformly in p, since it only uses residues of p mod small primes.)
why: A genuinely pointwise-in-p statement: for any fixed p and X ≥ (log p)^A, almost all C ≤ X have ω(4Cp+1) ≥ 6 (indeed ≈ log log Xp). So 'poor' failures are a vanishing fraction of C. Combined with the Kneser dichotomy, ES(p) would follow if 'periodic rich failures' could be shown not to happen for ALL C — a cleaner target (Galois-type: 'for some C, the prime factors of 4Cp+1 generate a subgroup containing −1 AND the subset-product set is not periodic-avoiding').
first_step: Prove the Turán–Kubilius bound for ω(4Cp+1), C ≤ X, uniform in p (standard; write it out with explicit constants); then count 'rich failures' empirically for p ≤ 10⁵ to see whether they are rare.
refs: Halberstam, 'On the distribution of additive number-theoretic functions' (1955)

title: Rich-failure structure: when ω(4Cp+1) ≥ 6 and −1 ∉ D, is D ⊂ H for an index-2 subgroup H (i.e. all prime factors lie in the kernel of one odd character)?
connection: Kneser-periodic failures with nontrivial stabiliser; the simplest is 'all factors in ker χ for an odd χ'. If rich failures are ALWAYS of this form, then: ES(p) fails ⟹ for every C with rich 4Cp+1 there is an odd character χ_C mod 4C with χ_C(q) = 1 for all q | 4Cp+1 — i.e. 4Cp+1 is a 'norm' from the quadratic field of χ_C. Then 4Cp+1 ∈ N(K_C) for every rich C — a family of 'simultaneous norm' conditions on linear forms in C, controlled by half-dimensional sieves over C (pointwise in p!): #{C ≤ X : 4Cp+1 is a norm from K_C} — but K_C varies with C, so the sieve is over a varying family; still each condition has 'density 1/√log' heuristically and the expected number of C ≤ X satisfying it is X/√log X ≪ X — but we need to show it's < (number of rich C), i.e. that NOT ALL rich C are norms, which requires the sieve LOWER bound… no: we need an upper bound on #{C: 4Cp+1 is a norm from K_C} < #{rich C} ≈ X. An upper bound ≪ X/√log X·const would suffice for X large! The catch: uniformity in p and the varying K_C. Promising structure.
why: If the dichotomy holds empirically and the sieve upper bound is provable uniformly, this is a *pointwise* proof sketch: 'poor C are few (Turán–Kubilius), norm-type C are few (half-dimensional sieve over varying fields), so some C is rich and non-norm ⟹ its subset-product set is non-periodic and large... ⟹ contains −1?' — the last step is the gap (large non-periodic D need not contain −1). Needs Kneser + a counting argument: |D| ≥ ω + 1 is too weak; but for non-periodic D the Kneser/Kemperman structure might force |D| ≥ φ(4C)/2 + 1 (if D·D ⊂ D-like); then D ∪ (−D) covers the group... −1 ∈ D ⟺ 1 ∈ −D; hmm, D is a product set containing 1; −1 ∈ D iff... Let me record the chain and its gap honestly.
first_step: (1) Empirically test the 'rich failure ⟹ all factors in ker of one odd χ' claim for p ≤ 10⁵, C ≤ 300. (2) If it holds, write the sieve upper bound for #{C ≤ X : all prime factors of 4Cp+1 in ker χ_C for SOME odd χ_C mod 4C} with explicit uniformity. (3) Identify the exact gap between 'rich, non-norm' and '−1 ∈ D'.

title: The 'rich non-norm but −1 ∉ D' gap: does the subset-product set D of a rich 4Cp+1 with factors NOT all in one index-2 subgroup necessarily contain −1? Count counterexamples
connection: D is generated (as a subset-product set with multiplicities) by ω ≥ 6 elements of G = (ℤ/4C)^× not all in any index-2 subgroup (i.e. for every odd χ, some factor has χ(q) ≠ 1). Does D ∋ −1? Certainly ⟨factors⟩ ∋ −1? Not necessarily: factors could lie in an index-4 subgroup missing −1 (not index 2) — e.g. G = ℤ/2 × ℤ/4 with −1 = (0, 2) and factors in {0} × ... hmm (0,2) is in ⟨(0,1)⟩. Take G = (ℤ/2)³ (4C = 24: (ℤ/24)^× ≅ (ℤ/2)³, −1 ↔ some vector v); factors in a 2-dim subspace not containing v: index 2 — covered. In (ℤ/2)³ every proper subgroup missing v is inside an index-2 subgroup missing v (hyperplane avoiding v exists iff v ≠ 0 ✓). For general abelian G and element v of order 2: is every subgroup H ∌ v contained in an index-2 subgroup ∌ v? Yes: G/H is a finite abelian group with v̄ ≠ 0 of order 2; there is a character of G/H nontrivial on v̄ (characters separate points); its kernel is a subgroup of index 2 (if the character has order 2) — the character χ with χ(v̄) ≠ 1 has χ(v̄) = −1 (order-2 element), but χ may have order > 2; then ker χ has index > 2 but χ² ... hmm, need an index-2 subgroup: take χ of G/H with χ(v̄) = −1; the subgroup ker(χ) has index ord(χ), may exceed 2. Alternative: the set of characters trivial on H and nontrivial at v̄ — does it contain an order-2 character? In G/H ≅ ℤ/4 with v̄ = 2: the order-2 character χ(1) = −1 gives χ(2) = 1 — fails! So in ℤ/4, the subgroup H = {0} misses v = 2, but the only index-2 subgroup {0, 2} contains v. So: for G with a cyclic ℤ/4 summand in which −1 is the element 2, there are −1-free subgroups (like {0} or ones generated by elements of odd order) not inside any index-2 −1-free subgroup. (ℤ/4C)^× has such summands when e.g. 5 | C ((ℤ/5)^× ≅ ℤ/4). So the 'index-2' dichotomy is incomplete; the correct statement: factors generate a subgroup H ∌ −1 — any index. The sieve then has dimension 1 − |H|/φ ≥ 1/2 anyway (larger for smaller H) — fine. The gap item stands but with 'all factors in some −1-free subgroup H' instead of index 2.
why: Corrects the previous item's formulation (group-theoretic precision matters for the sieve) and shows the sieve dimension is ≥ 1/2 in all cases — the half-dimensional sieve is the WORST case.
first_step: Enumerate for 4C ≤ 400 the maximal −1-free subgroups of (ℤ/4C)^× and their indices; confirm the worst case is index 2 and the sieve dimension is ≥ 1/2.

title: The final gap, isolated: 'prime factors of 4Cp+1 generate a subgroup containing −1' vs 'some subset product (with the actual multiplicities) equals −1' — bound the failure of the latter given the former via the Davenport constant
connection: If the factors (with multiplicity e_q) generate a group containing −1, does some subset product equal −1? Not necessarily — multiplicities too small (e.g. −1 = q⁴ needs e_q ≥ 4). The Davenport constant D(G) (every sequence of length ≥ D(G) has a zero-sum subsequence) and its 'prescribed element' variants (Olson, 'every element is a subsequence product when the sequence is long enough and generates') give: if ω(N) ≥ D(G)+something and the factors generate G, then EVERY element of G is a subset product — in particular −1. D((ℤ/4C)^×) ≤ roughly 4C·(…); for ω ≈ log log — far smaller than D(G) ≈ 4C. So multiplicity-poverty is the binding constraint: the subset-product set has ≤ 2^ω ≈ (log p)^{log 2} elements, while the group has φ(4C) elements — for C ≫ (log p)^{0.7} the set can't cover and −1 ∈ D is a 'coincidence' of probability |D|/φ(4C). So the real battleground is C ≤ (log p)^{0.7}-ish where |D| ≥ φ(4C) is possible. Document this scale.
why: Pins the exact scale of C where 'structural' arguments (generation ⟹ coverage) can work: C ≤ (log p)^{log 2 − ε}... and shows that for larger C, success is probabilistic (1/φ(4C) per C, summing to log X — the familiar count). A proof must therefore either (i) handle small C structurally (covering-like; but 409 etc. show small C fail for some p) or (ii) handle the probabilistic regime, which is B3. Useful map.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10⁵ the smallest winning C and whether |D_C| ≥ φ(4C) at that C (structural regime) or not (probabilistic regime); fraction of primes won in each regime.

title: Zero-sum theory (EGZ, Davenport) cannot be applied by pooling prime factors across C — B2 in zero-sum language
connection: Zero-sum / Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv flavour: with multiplicities, the prime factors of Π_{C ≤ K} (4Cp+1) (pooled across C!) form a long sequence in… different groups (ℤ/4C)^× — no common group. But pooled across C with 4C | M for a fixed M (i.e., C | M/4), all live in (ℤ/M)^× via reduction, and a divisor a of some 4Cp+1 with a ≡ −1 mod M certainly has a ≡ −1 mod 4C. So: fix M = 4·lcm(1..K); pool all prime factors of 4Cp+1 for C | M/4; if the pooled sequence is long enough (≥ D((ℤ/M)^×)) and generates, EGZ-type theorems give a subset product ≡ −1 mod M — but the subset must come from a SINGLE 4Cp+1 to be a divisor. So pooling doesn't directly help; unless the pooled products correspond to divisors of Π_C (4Cp+1) — which IS a p-tied integer (a polynomial in p of degree K!), with modulus M. So: 'the polynomial P_K(p) = Π_{C|M/4}(4Cp+1) has a divisor ≡ −1 mod M' is a necessary-ish consequence… does it imply an ES certificate? A divisor of the product is a product of divisors of the factors; need all of it inside one factor. No. Record as a structured negative: pooling across C breaks the 'single integer' requirement — THIS is B2 in zero-sum language.
why: Shows precisely why zero-sum theory (which handles long sequences) doesn't apply: ES's sequences are short (ω ≈ log log) per integer, and pooling destroys the divisor structure. Clean statement of B2.
first_step: Write it up as a one-paragraph negative in the lane md; no computation needed.

title: Analogy: Erdős's 'every n > 1 is a sum of distinct unit fractions with denominators ≤ …' — the greedy/Bleicher–Erdős bounds on the number of terms vs denominators; the 3-term boundary
connection: The theory of representing rationals as sums of k unit fractions with denominators ≤ D (Bleicher–Erdős 'Denominators of Egyptian fractions') gives tradeoffs between k and D; ES is k = 3, D unconstrained; maybe a tradeoff theorem 'k = 3 with D ≤ n² always' is provable with the same tools in a weakened form (e.g., k = 3 for all n outside a set of size ≪ N/(log N)^A — the Vaughan line).
why: Historical method check.
first_step: Read Bleicher–Erdős 1976 'Denominators of Egyptian fractions' II and see the structure of their k-term bounds for a/n.

why: Meta/community lever; cheap.

title: Teaching lens: the cleanest 'why ES is hard' demo is p = 409 — build a one-page explainer and use it to brief new lanes/boards
connection: 409 is small enough to hand-check: every 4C·409 + 1 for C ≤ 10 can be factored by hand, each failure explained; yet 16·409 + 1 = 6545 = 5·7·11·17 has the c=2 Type II certificate 7·935 (7 ≡ 935 ≡ −1 mod 8). It shows the congruence-slack of c ≥ 2 concretely.
why: Improves future lane quality (shared concrete example); near-zero cost.
first_step: Write BRAINSTORM/example_409.md with the table of 4C·409+1, C ≤ 12, factorizations, residues mod 4C, and the c=2 rescue.

title: Check whether Type II with c ≥ 2 is itself just the C-form for a *composite* n: ff′ = 4c²dp + 1 with f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 (mod 4cd) ⟺ C-form certificate for n = cp with C = cd?
connection: C-form for n' = cp with C' = cd: 4C'n' + 1 = 4cd·cp + 1 = 4c²dp + 1 ✓ and a ≡ b ≡ −1 mod 4C' = 4cd ✓. So Type II for p with parameters (c, d) is EXACTLY the C-form for the multiple n = cp with parameter C = cd. Hence: ES(p) via Type II ⟺ some multiple cp of p has a C-form certificate; and a solution for cp gives one for p by scaling?? NO — scaling goes the other way (solution for n gives one for multiples). Hmm: C-form for cp gives 4/(cp) = 1/(C'uv) + 1/(cpC'v) + 1/(cpC'u) ⟹ multiply by c: 4/p = c/(C'uv) + 1/(pC'v) + 1/(pC'u) — first term c/(cd·uv) = 1/(duv) ✓ a unit fraction! So yes: a C-form certificate for cp with C' = cd yields 4/p = 1/(duv) + 1/(pcdv) + 1/(pcdu). Consistent. So full Type II ⟺ 'some multiple cp of p, with C a multiple of c, has a C-form certificate' — the slack is exactly 'pass to a multiple'.
why: Clean structural dictionary: the C-form is the 'primitive' statement and Type II is its closure under passing to multiples cp with C ∈ cℤ. For 409: n = 818, C = 2 works. So the C-form exceptional set E and ES relate by: ES(p) ⟺ ∃c: (cp, C ∈ cℤ)-C-form certificate. The 'C-form conjecture for all non-square n' (if true) would imply ES immediately (take c = 1); its failure at 409 shows the conjecture is false for primes — so the right C-form conjecture is 'for every n, some multiple cn has a C-form certificate with c | C' — which is just ES.
first_step: Record the dictionary; recompute: for each C-form exception p, the smallest c such that cp has a C-form certificate with c | C (409: c=2).

title: Is the e-slice form ('∃ e ≡ −p mod 4 with −1 ∈ {ab⁻¹ mod e : ab | N}') the right 'primitive' with no exceptions? Compute its exceptional set vs C-form's
connection: The repo's e-slice form is stated as ⟺ ES(p) (FRONTIER §1), with N = (p+e)/4 (Type II) or (pe+1)/4 (Type I). Unlike the C-form it is claimed equivalent; its one-parameter nature (e) vs the C-form's suggests the e-slice packs (c, d) into e. Verify the equivalence numerically and compute the smallest winning e for the exceptions 409, 577, …
why: Establishes which one-parameter form is exact; informs the 'dimension' items.
first_step: Implement the e-slice test; verify against brute-force ES for p ≤ 3000; report e_min for the four exceptional primes.
